overview: The Marathon County Infrastructure Committee met on November 5th, 2026 and took several significant actions, most notably approving an ordinance to allow ATV/UTV access on State Highway 34 and separately voting to request the state DOT approve flashing warning signs for that segment. The committee also received updates on the 2027 budget, the routine state highway maintenance agreement, the Wausau MPO long-range transportation plan, and IT department projects, though no votes were taken on those informational items.

discussions.body: The minutes were approved without discussion. A motion was made by Watson and seconded by Coyle. The motion carried on a voice vote.

discussions.item: 2027 Annual Budget Overview
discussions.body: County Administrator Leonard and HR/Finance/Property Committee Chair Robinson presented a brief overview, noting the deadline for proposed budget amendments was 8:00 a.m. the following morning for Finance Committee review before county board adoption. Robinson highlighted that one driver of budget growth is funding for the highway facility. No amendments were proposed and no votes were taken.

discussions.item: ATV/UTV Access on State Highway 34
discussions.body: Supervisor Gal raised safety concerns about ATV/UTV traffic mixing with high-volume truck traffic on State Highway 34, citing approximately 6,000 vehicles per day compared to the county's 1,500-vehicle threshold for county trunk highways, and noting that ATVs traveling at 35 mph would share the road with trucks doing 60 mph. Jeff Gates, a member of the public, stated that hundreds of riders would use the route and that the current detour adds roughly 25 minutes of travel time. DOT representative Mike Crutchmer confirmed the DOT reviewed the draft ordinance but noted he deferred to access engineer Rich Hendrick on specifics. Vice Chair Gal moved to approve the ordinance with a condition requiring flashing warning lights; Supervisor Dickinson argued the signage question was separate and moved to divide the question into two parts. After procedural discussion involving corporation counsel, the motion was split: the original ordinance was approved unanimously on a voice vote, and a separate motion requesting the state DOT approve flashing warning signage for the ATV route on State Highway 34 passed 5-2.

discussions.item: Safe Routes to School Program and Cronin Area Request
discussions.body: Commissioner Lang explained that Marathon County's historical practice is to co-sign Safe Routes to School applications rather than serve as the primary sponsor, as the primary benefit is local. He noted the next application window is fall 2027, and that North Central Regional Planning assists communities with applications. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Routine Maintenance Agreement Update
discussions.body: Commissioner Lang and DOT Operations Manager Mike Crutchmer reviewed the annual routine maintenance agreement under which Marathon County maintains state roads. Discussion focused on cost reimbursement concerns, particularly the dramatic increase in plow blade costs — from roughly $300 to $750 for a 3-foot blade — and the inadequacy of the 5-year rolling average reimbursement rate to keep pace. Supervisors Gal and Sybert asked for data on the county's overall financial partnership with the state. No vote was taken; staff was directed to gather reimbursement and cost-sharing figures.

discussions.item: MPO Long Range Transportation Plan Update
discussions.body: Staff member Lori presented the update, noting four roadway segments identified as Level of Service D: State Highway 153/Main Street between 4th and Old Highway 51, Bridge Street over the Wisconsin River, West Thomas Street between South 3rd and Cleveland Avenue, and Grand Avenue between Townline Road and Thomas Street. The draft plan will be released for public review later in November through December. No vote was taken.

discussions.item: CCIT Projects Update
discussions.body: CCIT Director Greg Klein highlighted open enrollment IT support for the city and county, an upgrade to NetMotion VPN software across 128 squad cars to meet new criminal justice encryption requirements, and ongoing transition of network support for the UWSP campus on River Drive ahead of a January 1st handoff. A question arose about the status of the former Marathon County Credit Union building on Thomas Street, with the administrator confirming the occupant has not yet vacated. No vote was taken.

committee: Marathon County Joint Extension, Education, Economic Development and Human Resources, Finance, and Property Committee
overview: The Marathon County Joint Extension, Education, Economic Development and Human Resources, Finance, and Property Committees met to consider a one-year operating lease for the former UWSP campus theater building with the Marathon Center for Arts and Culture (MCAC), and to review two new proposals for the River Drive properties. The committees approved the MCAC lease with a modification requiring the tenant to cover approximately $7,428 in annual building insurance costs, then voted to enter closed session to discuss negotiation strategy on the River Drive RFP responses.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Two speakers offered public comment. Jim Davo, Village Administrator of Kronenwetter, thanked county staff in the clerk's office, highway shop, and sheriff's department for their professionalism and cooperative work with the village. Gail Marshall, speaking by phone, urged the committees to reject the current RFP proposals for the River Drive properties, arguing the process had failed to produce meaningful results and recommending the county instead hire a commercial real estate broker — estimating a 3% commission would still yield 97% of sale proceeds to taxpayers. She also asked what the county currently insures the River Drive properties for.

discussions.body: Minutes were approved by both committees in separate motions. For the HR, Finance, and Property (HRFC) committee, Vice Chair Pool moved and Supervisor Watson seconded; it passed.

discussions.item: UWSP Campus Redevelopment Update and MCAC One-Year Lease
discussions.body: Administrator Chris Holman reported that a city feasibility study agreement is in place, building systems are being inventoried and winterized, and staff are working with the UW exit committee. The proposed one-year operating lease with the Marathon Center for Arts and Culture (MCAC) was presented to bridge the gap while MCAC finalizes its 501c3 property tax exemption with the state. Tim Parker, CEO of the Community Foundation of North Central Wisconsin and MCAC fiscal agent, told committees that 95% of office spaces are leased and theater bookings are at 60% through June, with January and February already full. Kurt Gibbs raised the issue of insurance costs, noting the building is insured for approximately $13 million and the annual premium is roughly $7,428; he argued that cost should be borne by the tenant. Vice Chair Pool moved to approve the lease with a modification directing staff to negotiate inclusion of the $7,428 insurance cost spread over monthly payments; the motion was seconded and passed.

discussions.item: River Drive RFP Proposals – Raise and Roast Cafe (Oswald)
discussions.body: Justin and Elena Oswald presented their proposal to purchase 210 River Drive for $1 to develop 'Raise and Roast Cafe,' envisioning an affordable community cafe on the ground floor and a fundraising event venue on the second floor, with free recreational activities and partnerships with downtown institutions. Holman noted the proposal has strong alignment with criteria for activating unused property, community benefit, and local ownership, with moderate alignment on job creation and tax base reactivation. No formal vote or counter-offer was made in open session.

discussions.item: River Drive RFP Proposals – VFW Post 388 Veterans and Community Campus
discussions.body: Tamara Sillers, VFW Post 388 events coordinator, presented the VFW's proposal to acquire all three River Drive buildings (210, 212, and 326) to create a veterans and community campus, with 210 as an event venue, 212 as a community lounge with mental health counseling space and bingo, and 326 as garage and storage. She noted the VFW vacated River Drive around 2017 and the move was a mistake for community connectivity. Supervisors questioned how the new model differs from the bar-and-restaurant model that led to the prior departure, the organization's current revenue sources, and its nonprofit status (501c19). Holman disclosed the appraised market value of the River Drive parcel at $2,268,000 (land $87,000, improvements $1,261,000 as of November 2025) and insurance values: 210 at $2,635,700, 212 at $3,734,400, and 326 at $1,271,100. The presiding chair expressed disappointment at dollar-sale proposals given significant county investment, stating an obligation to taxpayers to maximize return.

discussions.item: Motion to Enter Closed Session on River Drive RFP
discussions.body: Corp Counsel explained that closed session was appropriate to discuss negotiation strategy and potential counter-proposals without revealing the county's position to the proposing parties. Both committees voted separately by roll call to enter closed session pursuant to Wisconsin Statute 19.85(1)(e) for competitive or bargaining reasons, specifically consideration of RFP responses for River Drive property. Both roll call votes passed unanimously.

overview: The Wausau Economic Development Committee met on November 4th and took action on three substantive items: authorizing staff to prepare a TID 8 project plan amendment for infrastructure projects, approving the $1 purchase of a tax-delinquent property at 108 Myron Street for future affordable housing, and debating a deed restriction and resolution for city-owned property at 1300 Cleveland Avenue. The Cleveland Avenue item resulted in a procedural deadlock, with a 2-2 tie on the amended resolution, sending the matter to the full city council on November 24th with section 4 removed from the deed restriction.

discussions.body: A motion to approve was made by Alder Neil and seconded by Alder Killian (noted in transcript as 'Kellian'). No discussion occurred and the minutes were approved by voice vote.

discussions.item: TID 8 Project Plan Amendment
discussions.body: Director Fifick explained the amendment would authorize staff to engage a consultant to draft a project plan amendment for Tax Increment District 8, adding infrastructure project costs including lead service line replacement, asphalt overlay, 17th Avenue reconstruction, water and sewer upgrades, and traffic signal replacement. Alder Killian expressed she was not prepared to vote without knowing whether lead line replacement funding covered private or entire replacement, but the motion carried 3-1. Staff noted the item had already been approved 5-0 at the Finance Committee and was placed on the November city council agenda.

discussions.item: Purchase of County-Owned Property at 108 Myron Street
discussions.body: Staff member Tammy presented details on the tax-delinquent property, which has been vacant for years due to a broken pipe causing black mold, rendering it too dangerous to enter. The county approved the city's $1 offer unanimously on October 20th, with full county board consideration set for November 10th. Funding for purchase and demolition would come from Community Development Block Grant funds, not tax levy, with DPW performing the demolition. The end goal is disposition for affordable housing for income-qualifying households. Alder Killian expressed safety concerns about demolition given the black mold but said she would support the motion. Alder Lukans noted for viewers that CDBG/HUD funds, not taxpayer levy money, would be used. The motion carried unanimously by voice vote.

discussions.item: Deed Restriction and Resolution for 1300 Cleveland Avenue
discussions.body: Director Fifick and the committee debated a draft deed restriction prohibiting industrial uses on the city-owned property at 1300 Cleveland Avenue, while preserving existing non-conforming uses including Marathon County/Wausau Parks log and wood chip storage and DPW training approved by a 2024 resolution. Alder Tierney's written comments, read into the record by Director Fifick, argued that non-conforming uses should end and the property cleaned up as promised to neighbors. Parks representative Jamie testified that relocating log storage requires council direction on an alternative site of approximately one acre, noting the ongoing Emerald Ash Borer program creates continuous need. Mayor Diny reported that fire training had already been relocated, and miscellaneous DPW equipment and a trailer had been cleaned up. Alder Killian moved an amendment to remove section 4A from the deed restriction, discontinue DPW training by February 1st, and give Parks 6 months to relocate; that amendment failed 2-2. Chair Heniki then moved a narrower amendment to remove only section 4 from the deed restriction, which passed 3-1. The main motion on the resolution as amended then failed 2-2, sending the matter to the November 24th city council meeting with section 4 removed from the deed restriction and a redrafted resolution to be prepared by staff.

He described it as a 'status quo budget' and highlighted that net new construction growth of only 1.5% necessitated fee increases. Robinson also flagged a newly announced DNR PFAS community sampling grant with a 20% match requirement that the health department is considering, with the village of Maine identified as an area of particular concern due to impacted wells. Lance, the county administrator, asked committee members to contact his office before Friday at 8:00 a.m. if they wished to propose amendments for the finance committee's Monday meeting. No amendments were proposed by Health and Human Services.

discussions.item: CART and Mobile Crisis Services Expansion
discussions.body: Committee member Katie raised questions about the status of discussions to expand CART (Crisis Assessment Response Team). Lance reported that North Central Healthcare executive director Jason Hake had inquired about CART expansion but that it was not built into the published budget. He noted modifications are being made to increase availability of North Central Healthcare crisis professionals for community response when law enforcement requests assistance. Supervisor John added that discussions with the sheriff's and police departments have shifted focus from CART expansion specifically toward broader mobile crisis service expansion, with a grant funding evaluation ongoing.

discussions.item: 2027 8521 Elderly and Disabled Transportation Grant Application
discussions.body: Staff presented the annual application for 8521 funds supporting elderly and disabled transit services in the county. The county is eligible to receive $366,060 from the state, requiring a local match of $73,201 covered through a partnership with Metroride, North Central Healthcare, and CPZ. Supervisor Ron asked where the local match funds were budgeted, and staff confirmed they are in CPZ's budget included in the 2027 budget before the board. The Transportation Coordinating Committee held a public hearing on October 21st with no public comments received and forwarded the application to this committee. Supervisor Rosenberg moved to approve forwarding the grant application to the county board; Supervisor Foot seconded, and the motion carried unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: 2027 Lead Service Line Funding Award from DNR
discussions.body: Director Lynman reported that the city received less DNR funding than anticipated and budgeted for. He explained that the absence of a lead service line replacement ordinance hurt the city's score on a second project, costing approximately $2 million in principal forgiveness. That $2 million will now need to be borrowed as additional debt. Lynman noted the matter will go to the finance committee on November 10th, coinciding with the full council's budget consideration, and may result in a budget amendment for additional borrowing. The chair noted that the alternative is to 'do less with what we've got.'

A commissioner identified as Handley questioned why no reimbursement was being sought; staff clarified the city owns no property being given up and will incur no costs, so reimbursement is not applicable. Motion was made by Martins, seconded by Hadley, and passed unanimously.

overview: The Marathon County Environmental Resources Committee held its November 3, 2026 meeting, conducting four rezoning public hearings and several town zoning reviews. The most significant action was the committee's decision to postpone a contested farmland preservation-to-low-density-residential rezoning request (MK7 Enterprises LLC in the Town of Marathon) to allow the town additional time to respond, following substantial opposition from neighbors, an attorney representing adjacent landowners, and a local farmer who owns surrounding acreage. discussions.item: 5A1: Weissaki Rezoning - General Agriculture to Rural Estate, Town of Green Valley
discussions.body: Staff presenter Garrett Pogle reported that both the Town of Green Valley and county staff recommended approval. Adjacent property owner William Kaiser raised concerns about an old dump on the property, including potential groundwater contamination and who would bear responsibility. Pogle explained that any new property owner inherits responsibility for existing violations, but that the dump predates the 10-year enforcement window, limiting the county's authority to act. The committee approved the rezoning to forward to the county board.

discussions.item: 5A2: Schultz Rezoning - Rural Residential to Rural Estate, Town of McMillan
discussions.body: Pogle reported that both the Town of McMillan and county staff recommended approval of the rezoning. No public comment was offered. The committee approved the motion without notable debate, with Supervisor Drebeck moving and Supervisor Shamborn seconding.

discussions.item: 5A3: MK7 Enterprises LLC Rezoning - Farmland Preservation to Low Density Residential, Town of Marathon
discussions.body: This was the most contested item of the meeting. Attorney Anders Helquist of Weld Riley Law Firm argued on behalf of adjacent property owners that the application failed all four statutory requirements to rezone out of farmland preservation, noting that the applicant's own application admitted two of the four standards were not met, that future land use maps show the parcel as agricultural/woodland, and that there were conflicts with surrounding agricultural uses. Local farmer Tyler Sehafer, who owns surrounding acreage, warned of road infrastructure inadequacy, grain bin noise conflicts, and noted that 100% of approximately 30 residents at a prior town meeting opposed the project. Land surveyor Dan Higinbotham, associated with the project, testified that wetland delineation was underway and soil evaluations were scheduled for the following Tuesday. Additional opposition came from Town of Marathon residents Randall Walcott and Karen Milbeck, who cited misleading communications about the project's intent and concerns about road damage from log trucks. Committee members debated extensively, with Chair Ritter noting a potential inconsistency with how the committee had handled a prior Town of Green Valley case based on future land use maps. Corporation Counsel advised that if a denial motion was made, it needed substantive reasons on the record. A motion to approve by Supervisor Sefelt failed for lack of a second. A denial motion by Supervisor Bro was ruled out of order by the chair after Corporation Counsel indicated it relied on factors not properly before the board (septic suitability). The committee ultimately voted to postpone the matter to no later than the January ERC meeting to give the Town of Marathon an opportunity to respond.

discussions.item: 5A4: Spencer Joint Revocable Trust Rezoning - Farmland Preservation to General Agriculture, Town of McMillan
discussions.body: Staff reported that both the Town of McMillan and county staff recommended approval. No public comment was offered. Supervisor Shamborn moved to approve based on findings of fact, conclusions of law, and the town's recommendation; the motion carried without notable debate.

discussions.item: 5B1 & 5B2: Town Zoning Changes - Town of Castle and Town of Weston
discussions.body: Both town-initiated zoning changes were presented by staff as having met all application requirements. Town of Castle sought a partial rezone from farmland to M1 Light Industrial; Town of Weston sought a rezone of Bowman Dairy Farm LLC property from Rural Residential 5-acre to Rural Residential 2-acre. Both were approved by the committee without public comment or significant debate.

discussions.item: 6A1: Data Center Ordinance Development Timeline
discussions.body: Director Lori Mski presented a timeline for developing a data center ordinance following a moratorium put in place in August. Staff described a research and survey phase currently underway, with outreach to surrounding counties and municipalities. The timeline targets a public hearing in June, well ahead of the one-year moratorium deadline, with a committee framework check-in planned at the six-month mark. No action was taken; the update was informational only.

discussions.item: Item 7: 2027 Budget Overview and PFAS Grant Opportunities
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson noted the prior day's budget presentation and reminded committee members that amendment requests were due by noon Friday. Robinson also highlighted two new DNR PFAS grant opportunities: a community-wide sampling grant for private wells and an individual private well sampling program, noting a 20% match requirement that could potentially be offset by in-kind contributions or staff time. Robinson thanked the committee for ongoing work on fee structures given levy restraints.

For item 5A3, attorney Anders Helquist (Weld Riley Law Firm) testified on behalf of the Marcott family and other adjacent property owners arguing denial on all four statutory grounds; local farmer Tyler Sehafer testified against the rezoning citing road infrastructure, agricultural conflicts, and near-unanimous community opposition at a prior town meeting; land surveyor Dan Higinbotham testified in a neutral/informational capacity about the project's due diligence process; Randall Walcott (Town of Marathon) opposed the rezone citing a flawed public process and asked the committee to send it back to the town; and Karen Milbeck (Town of Marathon) raised concerns about road damage from log trucks and potential tax increases.

title: Board (Budget Hearing)
overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors held its annual budget hearing on November 2, 2026 for the proposed 2027 budget. HR Finance Committee Chair Robinson and County Administrator Leonard presented a status quo budget that drops the property tax rate by one cent to $3.48, funds a new highway facility without new debt, and maintains current service levels. Three members of the public testified, two raising concerns about the county's Flock license plate reader camera system and one questioning the highway facility funding strategy.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Overview
discussions.body: HR Finance Committee Chair Robinson outlined the year-long budget development process including a 'bucket challenge' prioritization exercise by board members, review of fees, and direction to avoid new debt. Administrator Leonard presented key budget metrics: the property tax rate drops one cent to $3.48, equalized value grew 6.25%, net new construction was 1.545%, and the county ranks 13th lowest in per capita spending statewide. Leonard emphasized the highway facility funding plan — moving the $3.5 million North Central Healthcare payment onto the debt levy to avoid new borrowing for the nearly $55 million project — as the cornerstone of the budget.

discussions.item: Social Services Department Staffing Increases
discussions.body: Supervisor Sundowski questioned a proposed increase of 12 positions and roughly $4 million in the Social Services budget. Administrator Leonard and Social Services Director Christa explained that the Children's Long-Term Support (CLTS) social worker positions are fully federally funded through Medicaid billing and driven by state wait-list requirements, while the economic support specialist positions are funded through a state contract related to federal quality assurance requirements tied to the 'big beautiful bill.' Leonard clarified that positions are added incrementally as caseloads require, and that if funding streams disappear, the positions are eliminated without board action.

discussions.item: Highway Facility Funding Strategy
discussions.body: Supervisor Cavelli and Supervisor Nisth questioned the phased implementation of the highway facility debt levy strategy, citing concerns raised by former supervisor David Baker in public testimony. Baker had argued that placing the full $3.5 million NCHC payment on the debt levy in year one contradicted the phased approach described in Resolution 4926, and asked whether proceeds from property sales or reserves could reduce the $25 million funding gap. Administrator Leonard defended the approach, explaining that delay increases risk of having to borrow for other capital projects in 2029-2031, and that proceeds from the sale of West Street shop, 28th Avenue parcels, and the Thomas Street property (400 East Thomas) could shorten the inter-fund loan period but are best evaluated after the annual audit.

discussions.item: Flock License Plate Reader System — Budget Implications
discussions.body: Following public testimony from Courtney Olsen and Felix Gallow calling for defunding the Flock camera system, Supervisor Morash asked what budget options exist. Administrator Leonard explained that grant funds for the original five cameras are fully expended and $6,300 is in the sheriff's budget to continue that contract through the remainder of 2027; a second grant covering three cameras does not expire until March 2029 with no budget funds required. Sheriff Bip addressed the board, defending the technology as a legitimate law enforcement tool, stating that searches require a case number and are limited to specific personnel, that data is not shared with private entities, that audits occur twice monthly, and that the system is not used for immigration enforcement. Supervisor Robinson announced he had arranged a meeting between the sheriff and Gallow to work toward resolution. The board agreed to refer detailed discussion to the November 10 Public Safety Committee meeting.

discussions.item: User Fees and Equity Concerns
discussions.body: Supervisor Leur raised concerns that increased user fees disproportionately burden lower-income residents and asked whether the county tracks the impact of fee increases on service utilization. Administrator Leonard acknowledged the concern, noted that the marriage license fee was deliberately not increased at the county clerk's recommendation, and emphasized that fee-setting is ultimately a board policy decision. He also noted two additional fee changes — a professional services fee in the medical examiner's office and minor solid waste adjustments — would be brought to the board before final budget adoption.

publicComment: Three speakers testified at the formal public hearing. Courtney Olsen, executive director of a domestic violence agency, asked the board to amend the 2027 budget to prohibit county funds from being used for Flock or any license plate reader contract without a public hearing and board vote, and to request a corporate counsel opinion on board authority and county liability. Felix Gallow, also a Wausau resident, asked the board to prohibit budget funds from going to Flock without additional board study, and requested the sheriff commit to mandatory audits with oversight, quarterly public reports, and limiting data sharing to adjacent jurisdictions, state patrol, and DCI. David Baker of Kronenwetter supported the new highway facility and the no-new-debt strategy but questioned why the full $3.5 million payment was placed on the debt levy in year one rather than phased in, and asked the board to consider using property sale proceeds and reserves to reduce the $25 million funding gap.

title: Common Council Meeting
overview: The Wausau Common Council held its October 27, 2026 meeting, addressing a wide range of items including a detailed stormwater utility feasibility study presentation, routine resolutions, and a significant debate over the city's Flock license plate reader camera system. The council voted 8-2 to suspend rules and ultimately passed a resolution directing the appropriate city department to cease use of Flock data and physically cover all Flock cameras within two business weeks, reflecting sustained public and council pressure over privacy and data misuse concerns.

discussions.body: Mayor Diny read proclamations for Domestic Violence Awareness Month (October 2026) and Crash Responder Safety Week (November 2–6). Representatives from the Women's Community, identified as Shannon and Tess, were present for the domestic violence proclamation but declined a formal presentation. The crash responder safety proclamation was noted as being presented to the fire department later in the week.

discussions.item: Stormwater Utility Study and Stormwater Quality Management Plan Presentation
discussions.body: Justin Gataski of Strand Associates presented a two-part report: an update to the city's stormwater quality management plan and a stormwater utility feasibility study, both funded 50% by a Wisconsin DNR grant ($170,000 total project cost). Gataski explained the city currently meets total suspended solids reduction requirements (26.5% vs. 20% required) but falls significantly short on total phosphorus reduction (20.3% vs. 68.6% required under the Wisconsin River TMDL). The team recommended Alternative 2—constructing five structural best management practices (wet ponds) combined with water quality trading with neighboring MS4 communities—as the best path to compliance. Gataski also outlined a stormwater utility framework, estimating a cost of $100–$175 per year per equivalent runoff unit (ERU) for residential properties, with 36,265 total ERUs in the city. Alderperson Lukans asked about artificial turf and non-paying entities (schools, nonprofits) under a utility model; Gataski confirmed those entities would pay under a utility system. Alderperson Hanicki asked about likely resident concerns, with Gataski emphasizing the need for public education about the equity benefits of shifting from tax-based to fee-based funding.

discussions.item: Minutes Approval: October 13, 2026
discussions.body: A motion was made and seconded (second from True Blood) to approve the minutes. No questions or debate were raised and the minutes were approved by voice vote.

discussions.item: Public Comment on Flock Cameras and Boulevard Planting
discussions.body: Six members of the public spoke. Barbara [last name unclear] and others supported the proposed terrace beautification subcommittee and boulevard planting. Courtney Olsen, executive director of a domestic violence agency and chair of the Wisconsin Domestic Violence Fatality Review Initiative, urged the council to vote yes on Item 9 to end Flock camera use, citing stalking risks, documented officer misuse in Milwaukee and Menasha, and noting that public health and safety voted 5-0 and finance removed the $50,000 Flock line from the 2027 budget. Felix Gallow (1206 Highland Park Blvd.) and Carrie Morola (1025 Everest Blvd.) also urged the council to cover and end the Flock system. Danielle Fischer (1212 Highland Park Blvd.) asked the council to discontinue Flock immediately and not fund any like technology going forward.

discussions.item: Consent Agenda (less two pulled items)
discussions.body: Items 26-0707 (full-time HR coordinator) and 26-1013 (terrace beautification special committee) were pulled for separate consideration. The remaining consent agenda was approved on a motion from Watson, seconded by Neil, passing 10-0.

discussions.item: File 26-0707: Full-Time Human Resources Coordinator Position
discussions.body: Alderperson Watson pulled this item, expressing concern that adding a position before an upcoming comprehensive organizational audit could lead to a hire that later must be let go, and asked whether contracted services could serve as a bridge. Alder Tyranny defended the position, stating the HR department is 'barely treading water' and would go underwater if they lost one more person without help. Police Chief [unnamed] clarified that a $10,000 professional development allocation in the fiscal note represents shared savings from bringing crossing guard services in-house, saving the city roughly $40,000–$50,000 annually. Alder Martins noted the city's annual financial auditor had just urged better capture of institutional knowledge. Alder Heni confirmed the HR committee approved the position unanimously. The motion passed 9-1.

discussions.item: File 26-1013: Terrace Beautification Special Committee
discussions.body: Alderperson Larson pulled this item, expressing concern about adding more government and raising questions about public health, tree maintenance interference, and tall grass. Alderperson Trublood (chair of infrastructure and facilities) clarified the current boulevard planting ordinance dates to the 1970s and is vague, and that this temporary subcommittee—modeled after Madison's ordinance—would clarify it rather than create new bureaucracy. Alder Lukans confirmed the sustainability committee had been involved in developing the concept. The council approved the terrace beautification special committee by unanimous voice vote.

discussions.item: File 26-0706: Data Centers Zoning Ordinance (Reconsideration)
discussions.body: The council first voted 8-2 to reconsider the previously passed data centers zoning ordinance. On the main motion, Alder Lukans asked whether utility capacity verification was built into the ordinance; Planning Director Edmonson confirmed the ordinance requires applicants to submit energy, water, wastewater, and sound reports to assess utility capacity before a conditional use permit is granted and that the city could deny or require infrastructure upgrades. Alder Heni raised concerns about applicants self-sourcing favorable studies, and Edmonson said the city can contract for independent studies at the applicant's expense. Alder Martins asked about NDAs, and Edmonson said she is generally not in favor of NDAs as they complicate transparency, and the city attorney would need to review any NDA before signing. The ordinance was approved 9-1.

discussions.item: File 26-1014: Safe Drinking Water Revolving Loan Program Reimbursement Resolution
discussions.body: A resolution declaring official intent to reimburse expenditures from the Safe Drinking Water Revolving Loan Program for the FY 2027–28 lead service line replacement program was moved by Watson and seconded by Slantsky. No discussion was raised and it passed 10-0.

discussions.item: Item 9: Resolution to Cease Use of Flock Data and Cover Flock Cameras
discussions.body: Following an 8-2 vote to suspend the rules, the council debated at length a resolution directing the Wausau Police Department to cease using Flock data and cover all cameras. Police Chief [unnamed] raised concerns about the specific wording directing the police department to 'climb poles,' clarified Flock owns the cameras and contract language prohibits tampering, and asked for a legal opinion on authority. City Attorney Ann [last name inaudible] and a colleague confirmed the council has authority to direct the mayor (as chief executive) to order coverage of the cameras but not to directly order the police chief to do so physically. Alder Watson moved an amendment directing the appropriate city department—under instruction of the chief executive officer—to physically cover the cameras within two business weeks; this passed 9-1. Alder Trublood expressed concern about breaching the contract, while Alders Lukans, Tierney, and Martins argued the original vote was made without knowledge of Flock's data misuse and AI expansion and that public trust demanded action. The chief confirmed that access to Flock data can be restricted via a software switch, but uncovered cameras continue to capture and store images for 30 days even without city access. The main motion as amended passed [tally not explicitly stated in transcript before cut-off].

publicComment: Six residents spoke during public comment. Barbara [last name unclear] expressed support for the terrace beautification initiative. Courtney Olsen (Highland Park Blvd.), executive director of a domestic violence agency and statewide fatality review chair, urged the council to vote yes on Item 9 to end Flock camera use, citing stalking-related misuse by officers in Milwaukee and Menasha, noting 42 Wisconsin agencies have ended or decided to end Flock, and warning that the city's own contract limits Flock's liability to one year of fees while Wausau County faces lawsuits over warrantless Flock searches. Felix Gallow (1206 Highland Park Blvd.) urged the council to support ending Flock and praised the fire department's community prevention work as a model for policing. Carrie Morola (1025 Everest Blvd.) called Flock an unnecessary expense and urged the council to cover the cameras and redirect funds to resident needs. Danielle Fischer (1212 Highland Park Blvd.) urged the council to discontinue Flock immediately and not fund any similar technology going forward. A fifth speaker, Chad Felix Gallow [unclear if separate speaker], made brief supportive remarks.

discussions.item: Presentation of 2025 Financial and Single Audit by Maldin Jenkins CPAs
discussions.body: Lucas Hand, CPA and director at Maldin Jenkins, presented the city's fiscal year 2025 audit results, reporting a clean, unmodified opinion on both the financial statements and the single audit compliance report. The city ended the year with total net position of $300.3 million, general fund revenues of $46.3 million versus expenditures of $47 million, and an overall net position increase of $12.7 million. One single audit finding was noted — a significant deficiency for suspension and debarment recordkeeping, which Hand described as a common checklist issue with no impact on federal funds. Hand also issued a management point (not an audit finding) recommending cross-training and documentation of key processes, noting that finance department knowledge is concentrated in a limited number of individuals. Alderperson Hincki asked Hand to expand on succession planning concerns, and the chair asked about upcoming GASB standards 103 and 104, with Hand expressing confidence the city is prepared.

discussions.item: Approving Fiscal Year 2026 Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant and Interlocal Agreement with Marathon County
discussions.body: Captain Graham presented the annual formula-based federal grant of $15,920, awarded jointly to the City of Wausau and Marathon County, requiring an interlocal agreement for Marathon County to receive funds. The grant is historically used to fund equipment in the regional forensic lab, such as GrayKey or Cellebrite technology. No significant debate occurred and the item was approved unanimously.

discussions.item: Approving Budget Amendment for 415 South 1st Avenue Development Agreement with Gorman Company (Westside Commons)
discussions.body: Patrick from economic development explained that Gorman Company had met all milestones under their development agreement, including minimum spend, project completion, and obtaining 90% occupancy for three or more months, as well as securing permanent financing. The committee approved a $650,000 Tax Increment Grant (TIG) payment to Gorman Company, which will come before the full council as a budget modification. The vote carried without notable debate.

discussions.item: Authorizing Staff to Prepare Project Plan Amendment for Tax Increment District 8
discussions.body: The chair described this item as moving private-side lead service line replacement costs to TID 8 where appropriate, along with 17th Avenue reconstruction and asphalt overlay within the district — topics previously discussed during budget sessions. The motion passed without discussion.

discussions.item: Approving Agreement Between City of Wausau and Wausau Cemetery Association
discussions.body: Staff presented a revised, consolidated cemetery agreement reflecting a current annual payment of $76,721.44 and new language giving the public works director authority to offer surplus vehicles to the cemetery at no cost on a right-of-first-refusal basis. Parks Director Jamie raised significant concerns about a new, large tree removal and stump grinding request from the cemetery — nine trees and 23 total stumps — which would take city urban forestry crews approximately two weeks, raising questions about liability for headstone damage, worker safety on non-city property, and cost. Alder Watson moved to table the agreement until the next finance committee meeting pending cost estimates, a map of the requested work, copies of the prior agreements, and potential cemetery board attendance; Alder Hincki seconded. The motion passed with one nay and the chair abstaining, citing his wife's service on the cemetery board. Items G and H were also pulled to the next meeting.

discussions.item: Approving 3% Increase to Hangar Lease Agreements at Wausau Downtown Airport Beginning 2027
discussions.body: The committee discussed a 3% rate increase for T-hangar leases at Wausau Downtown Airport, with current monthly rates ranging from approximately $3 to $6 depending on hangar size. Staff noted the airport is below market compared to peer facilities. Alder Hincki asked for more detail on how rates are set and how far behind market the city is. Alder Neil moved to approve; Alder Hincki seconded. The item passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Approving Multi-Year Budget Amendment for Wausau Fire Department Apprentice Program Paid by Federal Grant
discussions.body: Fire Chief Jeremy explained this was a bookkeeping amendment to create a budget line matching the previously approved federal apprenticeship grant, enabling staff to track spending across the three-year grant period. He confirmed all costs — including gear, equipment, and collaboration with Northcentral Technical College — are covered within the grant for two cohorts of nine apprentices each. Alder Hincki asked whether apprentices would have a direct path to city employment; the chief clarified they would need to apply for open positions through the standard process. The motion from Hincki with a second from Tyranny passed unanimously.

The board approved a final tax levy of $44,385,271—the same as the prior year—with a mill rate of $6.26 per thousand, 28 cents less than projected at the annual meeting. discussions.item: Red Granite Charter School Principal Presentation
discussions.body: Principal Ma Mangan presented on the school's third year of operation as a public Waldorf school, reporting approximately 65 students including 24 new 4K students, 100% teacher retention, and expansion to a second early childhood classroom. Board members, including one identified as Pat McKee, praised word-of-mouth marketing and noted the school's no-screen and outdoor-focused approach as enrollment drivers. discussions.body: Assistant Superintendent Dr. Elizabeth Channel and Buildings and Grounds Director Ryan Ormansky presented a first phase of modifications allowing 501(c)(3) organizations, Title 36 youth groups (such as scouts), and governmental agencies to request fee waivers for facility use during normal operating hours (6:30 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.). discussions.item: Hmong Language Offering
discussions.body: Director of Secondary Education Dr. John Tossky and Dr. Cwell presented findings on potentially offering Hmong as a language course, noting highlights such as community engagement, college credit potential, and innovative positioning, as well as challenges including declining enrollment in existing global languages, difficulty finding and retaining a licensed Hmong teacher (no licensure programs exist in Wisconsin for the DPI 1389 license), and curriculum development costs. Board members Charles Burger and others asked about Wave virtual delivery, summer program pilots, and demand measurement. Lance Trollop and Pat McKee cautioned that adding a language amid declining enrollment and budget constraints could come at the expense of existing language offerings. Board President Bouché noted Act 31 obligations regarding Southeast Asian heritage language instruction. The board directed staff to gauge student interest before the next presentation on this topic; no vote was taken.

discussions.item: Tech Ed Course Approvals - Digital Design and Manufacturing
discussions.body: CTE Coordinator John Wy presented a restructuring of the graphics and Fab Lab pathways, combining Graphics 1 and Fab Lab into a new 'Digital Design and Manufacturing' course, renaming Graphics 2 to 'Graphic Design and Software,' and reducing Graphics 3 (Warrior/Lumberjack Graphics) from a double block to a single block while retaining NTC dual credit. Teachers and administration were reported to be fully supportive. The motion to recommend approval to the full board carried.

discussions.item: Academic Career Plan (ACP) 2026-27
discussions.body: CTE Coordinator John Wy presented the district's ACP in alignment with PI26, highlighting student success stories, innovative pathways including aviation, robotics, auto collision, and math and construction, and two goals: expanding work-based learning participation by 10% and reducing undecided seniors from 11-15% to under 8%. Board members praised the presentation and noted the importance of ACP for community awareness. The motion to recommend approval to the full board carried.

discussions.body: Dr. Kempky reported no increases to student fees for 2027-28, noting ongoing monthly collaboration with Dr. Channel and athletic directors on athletics funding. The motion to recommend approval to the full board carried with opposition noted.

discussions.body: Dr. Channel presented the finalized 2026-27 budget, reporting a mill rate of $6.26 per thousand—28 cents less than projected at the annual meeting—driven by increased equalization aid and increased property values. Enrollment declined by 215 students from fall 2025 to fall 2026, with a three-year rolling average down 133 students. The district is approximately $13 million behind inflationary pace, representing a cumulative $71 million deficit since 2011. The private school voucher aid deduction totals $4,629,595, adding about $65 per $100,000 home. The board approved the final budget and set the tax levy at $44,385,271—the same as the prior year—while defeasing approximately $11 million in debt. A board member requested additional data on equalized value trends, transportation reimbursements, and special education enrollment for use in legislative discussions.

title: Community Life & Public Safety
overview: The Village of Weston Community Life & Public Safety Committee met and addressed code enforcement updates, fire/EMS/police department reports, a new liquor license recommendation, and a key vote on a proposed pedestrian crosswalk at Newport Avenue and Business 51. The committee approved recommending a Class B beer and liquor license for Trailside Sports Bar and Grill, and voted to instruct the DOT to include the Newport Avenue crosswalk in design plans for the Business 51 reconstruction project, with one dissenting vote.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Jim Po of 512 Girl Street, Weston, offered public comment. He humorously presented a wooden number five to recognize 6202 Ross Avenue for being on the code enforcement list for five years, calling it 'the pinnacle of commitment to municipal nuisance.' He also raised substantive questions about the proposed Business 51 crosswalk, questioning whether the $60,000 expenditure was a need or a want, how many residents would actually use it, and whether corridor businesses had been consulted or invited to the meeting.

discussions.item: Code Enforcement Update
discussions.body: Staff presented a code enforcement report showing over 100 cases opened annually, with 23 active cases older than one year including one dating to 2021 at a property with abandoned vehicles and solid waste. Code enforcement staff explained the 2021 case involves family deaths and medical issues that slowed compliance, but that the property owner's daughter has been cooperating and making progress this summer. Committee members questioned whether leaving resolved cases open was accurate or inflating case counts, and debated at what point long-standing cases should be escalated to legal action. Staff maintained that as long as progress is being made, they continue working cooperatively rather than pursuing court action, which can be costly and may not address the root cause.

discussions.item: Fire, EMS, and SAFER Report
discussions.body: Fire Chief presented a written report. A committee member asked about mold at Station 2, and Chief confirmed there had been water leaks which are believed to be fixed, with abatement and repair contractors lined up. Omni Glass had conducted exterior assessments and tracked the water intrusion to a second-floor window that was subsequently sealed.

discussions.item: Police Department / Metro Report
discussions.body: Police Chief reported 2,290 calls for service, 54 crashes, and 596 traffic stops. Committee members noted a spike in crashes particularly in the Brill area attributable to highway construction causing frequent lane changes. The Village of Weston recorded 24 crashes compared to 12 in Schofield and 14 in Rothschild.

discussions.item: Humane Officer Training Presentation
discussions.body: Officer Kum Mua, a night-shift officer with approximately 14 years of experience, presented on her 40-hour humane officer certification training through the Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection. She described how animal cases differ from typical law enforcement calls in that they require extensive follow-up monitoring and are often subjective, requiring on-site assessment of animals including physical inspection. Chief noted the department has three certified humane officers who handle major cases while other officers manage routine animal calls. Discussion also covered animal registration compliance, with staff noting it is somewhat easier now that registration is handled in-house rather than through a third-party online system.

discussions.item: Class B Beer and Liquor License – Doug's LLC / Trailside Sports Bar and Grill
discussions.body: Village Clerk Pam Bream confirmed online that all required paperwork, background checks, and publication fees had been submitted and a provisional license issued. The committee moved to recommend approval of the Class B beer and Class B liquor license for Doug's LLC doing business as Trailside Sports Bar and Grill. The recommendation will go to the full Village Board at its November 16th meeting for final approval.

discussions.item: Business 51 Reconstruction – Newport Avenue Pedestrian Crossing
discussions.body: Village engineer Mike presented the DOT's planned reconstruction of Business 51, currently scheduled for 2030-2031, and asked whether the committee wanted to include a pedestrian refuge island crossing at Newport Avenue in the design. The village's cost share would be roughly one-third, estimated at $40,000–$60,000 at today's prices. He noted the road median at Newport is currently only four feet wide and people are observed crossing diagonally without a safe refuge. Public works endorsed including it in design. Committee members generally supported it for future-proofing given nearby businesses, apartments, and the junior high school, with one member noting it would set up the corridor for potential future development. One member voted in opposition. The committee voted to direct the DOT to move forward with designing the crosswalk into the project plans.

publicComment: One speaker offered public comment in person: Jim Po of 512 Girl Street, Weston. He humorously recognized 6202 Ross Avenue for its five-year presence on the code enforcement list and presented the committee with a wooden number five. He also raised concerns about the proposed Business 51 pedestrian crosswalk, questioning the cost-benefit given limited residential density on the west side of Business 51, and asked whether affected businesses had been formally notified or invited to comment. No one commented online or from the audience.

title: Parks and Recreation Committee
overview: The Weston Parks and Recreation Committee met to discuss aquatic center repairs and financials, approve the Machm Miller Park master plan, and review the Kennedy Park master plan and quarterly update. The committee voted unanimously to recommend the Machm Miller Park master plan to the Village Board, and held substantive discussion about the future of Kennedy Park development, including the farmers market location, a potential hockey facility in the northwest corner, and fundraising priorities for a future concession stand.

discussions.body: The minutes from the September 28, 2026 meeting were moved and seconded without discussion. The committee approved them unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Public Comments
discussions.body: Two public comments were received. Tony Case, a farmers market vendor from Ringle, made three suggestions to improve traffic flow and parking at the Kennedy Park farmers market lot, including widening the entrance to three lanes, adding a permanent directional sign to overflow parking, and exploring use of a strip of land near the power boxes for additional parking. An online commenter identified as Jim criticized the committee sharply, calling out the lack of a Friends of Kennedy Park financial update in the meeting packet, the absence of cost estimates or recommendations in the aquatic center repair staff report, and the failure to include a timeline or realistic financial impact for the Machm Miller Park plan, stating the estimated total cost exceeds $4.137 million and calling the omissions 'unacceptable.'

discussions.item: Update on Aquatic Center Repairs
discussions.body: Staff member Sean reported that contracts are in place with New Pools for leak detection ($12,000) and for motors, pumps, and valves ($123,000-$128,000), both previously approved. Leak detection identified a suspected area near the play structure, close to a previous leak location, and deck removal began to verify it; no cost estimate for repairs was available when the packet was sent Wednesday. Staff explained the pressure-check sonar method used for leak detection and noted the pool has been winterized with RV antifreeze, with water still needing to be returned to the deep well.

discussions.item: Update on Aquatic Center Financials
discussions.body: Sean presented the current operational budget showing revenues of $246,000 against a budget of $226,000, and expenditures of $230,000 against a budget of $256,000, for a positive variance of approximately $16,000 revenue over expenditures compared to budget. The pool special revenue fund balance stands at approximately $29,000, which would grow to $45,000 with the $16,000 surplus, pending remaining utility and winterization costs through December. Staff noted the operational budget does not include capital expenses such as the outside contractor contracts, which run through the CIP.

discussions.item: Machm Miller Park Master Plan and Cost Estimates
discussions.body: Staff presented the most recent version of the Machm Miller Park master plan and cost estimates, noting the plan is not yet approved and there is therefore no current fiscal impact. The total estimated cost is high and the plan is envisioned as a 10-to-20-year roadmap for consistency as committee membership changes. Notable additions from public input included tennis and basketball courts; staff flagged that the cost estimate omits redoing existing walking paths, only pricing new trail sections at approximately $90,000. A committee member moved to recommend the plan to the Village Board, which was seconded by Roger, and the motion passed unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Kennedy Park Master Plan and Quarterly Update
discussions.body: Staff provided a quarterly update noting Friends of Kennedy Park received $17,500 from youth baseball and nearly $4,000 from concession stand proceeds from a softball tournament, bringing the estimated community foundation balance to approximately $124,939.55, with $98,000 dedicated to lights installed at Ray Jack field on October 19-20. The second annual Glow Games indoor event is scheduled for February 20, 2027. Jimmy Olson of the Friends of Kennedy Park addressed the committee, confirming fundraising is ongoing with no brakes applied, and that internally the group sees a concession stand as the next major goal, while remaining flexible given uncertainty about the farmers market location and a potential hockey facility in the northwest corner. Committee members discussed moving the farmers market to the northwest corner near the proposed hockey facility off Altaverie and Newport, which would allow back-to-back ball diamonds to remain and provide a flatter, potentially covered space for market vendors. The committee reached informal consensus that the farmers market will likely remain at field 2 for the next year, the next development step will take more than a year, and fundraising focus should shift toward a concession stand building, with village consideration of phase 2 parking improvements.

publicComment: Two public comments were received. Tony Case (226305 County Road 2, Ringle, WI) spoke in person as a farmers market vendor, offering three suggestions: widening the Kennedy Park parking lot entrance from two lanes to three (one in, two out) to address bottlenecks; adding a permanent mounted sign directing patrons to overflow parking and additional handicap spaces; and exploring a strip of land near the power boxes adjacent to the ball field for 20-35 additional parking spots. An online commenter identified as Jim criticized the committee for omitting a Friends of Kennedy Park financial update from the packet, for providing no cost estimate or recommendation on aquatic center repairs, and for stating 'none' as the financial impact of the Machm Miller Park plan despite estimates exceeding $4.137 million, calling the omissions a failure of customer service to the village's 16,000 residents.

title: Finance Committee Budget Session #4 Meeting
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee held its fourth budget session for the 2027 budget on October 20, 2026, working through a series of amendments to the proposed budget including removing Flock camera funding, redirecting the city administrator allocation toward an audit, and approving new fee schedules. The committee approved several amendments by voice vote, including eliminating $50,000 in Flock ALPR camera funding, $45,000 in alley paving, $150,000 for the city administrator position, and $20,000 in trail planning, while rejecting a proposal to remove $25,000 for street tree planting.

discussions.item: Public Comment — Flock ALPR Cameras
discussions.body: Six members of the public spoke, all urging the committee to remove Flock camera funding from the 2027 and 2028 budgets. Felix Gallow, citing the Wisconsin Supreme Court and Flock's own chief legal officer's blog post, argued that non-appropriation carries negligible litigation risk and that over a dozen Wisconsin agencies have ended Flock contracts without being sued. Courtney Olsen, executive director of a domestic violence agency, warned that ALPR systems can be misused as stalking tools, citing cases in Milwaukee and Menasha. Mary Clus, Danielle Fischer, and Carrie Morola also spoke in favor of removal, with speakers noting the Public Health and Safety Committee had voted 5-0 the prior evening to recommend striking the Flock appropriation.

discussions.item: Property Record Maintenance Fee
discussions.body: City Assessor Rick Rubo presented a proposal for new property record maintenance fees, noting that approximately 12 other Wisconsin municipalities have adopted similar fees to recoup staff time for updating physical and electronic property record cards when permits are issued and when parcels are split or combined. He described the administrative burden of processing condominium plat combinations affecting 55+ units. The committee approved the new fees by voice vote as an amendment to the fee schedule.

discussions.item: Updated Assessed Value and Tax Rate Impact
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne reported that the final assessed value came in at a 2.56% increase (approximately $464.9 million above estimates), significantly stronger than the projected 1%. This revised the estimated tax rate downward from $9.24 to $9.10 per $1,000, reducing the estimated annual tax impact on a $200,000 home from $9,973 to $7,152. The committee noted remaining tax rate unknowns pending school, technical college, and county levies.

discussions.item: Motor Pool Reconciliation
discussions.body: The finance director presented a 2027 motor pool reconciliation showing departmental charges totaling $4.018 million in the general fund and $4.5 million entity-wide, with budgeted revenues of $4.8 million, expenses of $3.5 million, capital purchases of $1.8 million, and a shortfall of $448,000. She noted the target to fully recover costs would require an additional $1.3 million but that a 2026 budget modification was anticipated and the general fund was performing well enough to support the fee structure for the next two years, though not solving the long-term problem.

discussions.item: Debt Service Scenarios and TID 8 Capital Projects
discussions.body: The finance director presented three debt financing scenarios for 2027 and 2028 infrastructure: a standard 10-year even amortization, a structured 10-year with reduced early payments, and a 15-year term. She recommended the structured 10-year approach to manage levy growth, noting the 2027 borrowing of approximately $6.365 million and 2028 borrowing of approximately $6.151 million. She also proposed amending the TID 8 project plan to include $2.5 million for lead service line replacement, $300,000 in asphalt overlay, and $250,000 for 17th Avenue design, projecting the district could close as early as 2035 with $9.3 million remaining even without new growth.

discussions.item: Alcohol License and Fee Schedule Changes
discussions.body: City Clerk staff reported that most alcohol license fees are capped by state statute, limiting the city's ability to increase them. Proposed changes included a modest increase to the Class A beer license, a new $100 late publication fee for licenses renewed after deadline, reducing the group publication fee from $30 to $25, adding a $150 late renewal fee, increasing the lapsed bartender license fee from $125 to $130, and reducing the alcohol premises amendment fee from $150 to $25 to increase compliance. The committee approved the alcohol and cigarette fee changes by voice vote as moved by Alder Tierney and seconded by Alder Watson.

discussions.item: Flock Camera Funding Removal — Budget Amendment
discussions.body: Alder Tierney moved to remove $50,000 allocated for Flock cameras from the 2027 budget and reallocate it to the motor pool rather than reduce the tax levy. After discussion about whether to place the funds in the police department, street maintenance, or elsewhere, the committee agreed the $50,000 would be reallocated within the general fund toward motor pool expenses in one of the underfunded departments. Mayor Doug Diny recommended keeping it within public safety for items like crowd control barricades. The motion was seconded by Alder Watson and approved by voice vote.

discussions.item: City Administrator Budget Line — $150,000 Amendment
discussions.body: Alder Tierney moved to remove the $150,000 budgeted for a city administrator, with discussion about redirecting those funds to support the recently council-approved city audit. Alders Watson and Hincki expressed support for using the funds for the audit, noting a third-party assessment should inform any future administrator hiring decision. The amendment was approved with the $150,000 moved from general government to the council's consulting services line item to serve as a placeholder for audit expenditures in 2027.

discussions.item: Alley Paving — $45,000 Removal
discussions.body: Alder Tierney moved to remove $45,000 for alley paving; Alder Hincki seconded. Public Works Director confirmed no petitions for alley paving in 2027 have been received, making the appropriation a placeholder; any future petitioners would simply be told to reapply for the 2028 budget. The amendment passed by voice vote.

discussions.item: Trail Planning — $20,000 Removal
discussions.body: Alder Tierney moved and Alder Hincki seconded removing $20,000 for trail planning, which was funded through TID-Today (TID near west side). Parks Director Feifer clarified the funding was intended to plan an extension of the Riverlife Trail on the MBX property for eventual 2028 construction. Alders Watson and Neil voted no, noting the funds came from TID revenues rather than the general tax levy. The motion passed 3-2.

discussions.item: Street Tree Planting — $25,000 Removal
discussions.body: Alder Hincki moved to remove $25,000 for street tree planting, seconded by Alder Watson, arguing it was inappropriate to incur 10-year debt for trees and suggesting cash funding instead. Alders Neil, Tierney (chair), and Watson strongly opposed removal, with Alder Neil invoking the Fulton Street reconstruction as an example of neighborhoods 'denuded' of trees and citing the city's duty to restore what was taken. Multiple members cited economic research on trees increasing property values. Alder Watson stated she seconded only to get the motion on the floor and would not support it. The motion failed 4-1, with only Hincki voting in favor.

discussions.item: TID 12 Tool Design Engineering — $150,000 Removal
discussions.body: Alder Tierney moved to remove $150,000 for tool design engineering in TID 12, characterizing it as desirable but deferrable. Alder Hincki seconded. Discussion was cut off in the transcript before a vote was recorded.

publicComment: Six residents spoke in opposition to Flock ALPR camera funding. Mary Clus (127 Kent Street) asked the committee to remove Flock from the budget citing privacy concerns and poor use of resources. Felix Gallow (1206 Highland Park) presented a legal analysis arguing non-appropriation is a routine discretionary tool under Wisconsin law, that Flock's own chief legal officer acknowledged municipalities retain discretion over appropriations, and that no Wisconsin agency that dropped Flock has been sued. Courtney Olsen (Highland Park Boulevard), a domestic violence agency executive director, warned ALPR systems can be misused as stalking tools, citing documented officer misuse cases in Milwaukee and Menasha, and outlined specific procedural steps for contract termination. Danielle Fischer (1212 Highland Park Boulevard) noted community support on social media for removing the cameras. Carrie Morola (1025 Everest Boulevard) framed removal as a double win — saving taxpayer money and rebuilding constituent trust.

title: Administrative Policy Committee and Village Board - Budget Workshop 2
overview: The Village of Kronenwetter held its second 2027 Budget Workshop covering public safety budgets (police and fire/EMS), TIF district updates, community development staffing, and a future debt service preview. The board's most significant action was recommending and approving keeping the contingency fund at $60,000 rather than the proposed $70,000, saving approximately $12 on a $200,000 home's village tax share. Village Administrator John Jacobs also previewed that the 2028 budget will likely require approximately a 20-cent tax rate increase to cover new debt service if the capital improvement program borrowing proceeds.

discussions.item: Historical Tax Rate and Equalized Valuation Overview
discussions.body: Village Administrator John Jacobs presented a historical chart showing the village's assessed and equalized tax rates since 2020, noting that at full equalized valuation the rate would drop from $4.26 to approximately $2.71-$2.80. He contextualized the village's rate against Marathon County, two school districts, and NCTC, noting the village represents only about 20-25% of a resident's total tax bill. He noted Marathon County's rate of $3.48 is higher than the village's proposed rate.

discussions.item: Port-a-Potty Budget and Vandalism
discussions.body: Staff presented a cost chart for port-a-potty options ranging from approximately $6,700 for six standard units to over $21,000 with ADA-accessible units. Staff recommended a combination of three regular and three ADA units as a reasonable middle ground. Officials identified Bushka Park and Friendship Park as the primary vandalism sites, noting most damage occurs during daytime hours and that the contracted vendor has a policy of pulling units if vandalism occurs. No formal vote was taken; the matter was flagged for parks committee review.

discussions.item: TIF District Administration Costs - Legal Guidance
discussions.body: Jacobs reported receiving guidance from financial advisor Ariana Schmidt of Ehlers clarifying that administrative costs, professional services, and DOR fees can continue through the maximum life of a TID even after the expenditure period ends, but no new capital costs can be incurred after that period. Jacobs also disclosed a correction: TID 1 and TID 4 expenditure periods ended in 2019, not 2024 as previously documented. TID 2 had special legislation allowing expenditures through 2024. All three TIDs can continue accruing administrative costs until closure.

discussions.item: Police Department Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Police Chief Terry [last name inaudible] presented a largely status-quo budget, noting the primary cost increases stem from funding two officers for a full 12 months versus a partial year. A $21,700 line for new officer startup costs was removed. Capital equipment was cut by $9,000. The chief noted a planned hire is expected mid-to-late December at earliest, which could yield some payroll savings. Crossing guard pay was raised to $20/hour to aid retention. A $1,500 full-body restraint wrap system was requested as new equipment. The municipal court clerk overlap budget for Diane's retirement transition was also discussed, along with a proposed municipal judge salary increase from $5,500 to $6,000 effective April 2027.

discussions.item: Fire and EMS Department Budget Presentation
discussions.body: Fire Chief Teresa O'Brien presented a budget with modest increases, primarily for radio replacement ($20,000 from fire budget, $5,000 from EMS) and $800 in additional training. EMS call volume is projected at 492-500 for 2026-2027, up from 420 budgeted, a 25% increase driven largely by mental health-related calls. The EMS wage budget of $68,546 is expected to run approximately $9,000-$10,000 over, requiring a budget amendment in November. O'Brien highlighted three supplemental grant funds — 2% fire dues, FAP EMS grant (~$35,000/year), and a fire donations fund — totaling approximately $70,000 in non-general-fund expenditures annually.

discussions.item: Community Development Staffing and Planning Tech Position
discussions.body: Jacobs noted savings in 2026 due to the gap between Pete's departure and Nathan's hiring on August 3rd. The planning technician position, funded from April 2026, remains unfilled, creating roughly $30,000 in 2026 savings. Two interviews have been conducted with candidates who have GIS experience. Planning commission meetings are proposed to increase from 12 to 16 annually, and zoning board of appeals from 2 to 4 meetings, resulting in modest cost increases. A $10,000 placeholder for a potential TID 5 feasibility study was recommended to remain in the budget.

discussions.item: TIF District Tax Increment and Distribution Center Impact
discussions.body: Jacobs presented estimated tax increment figures: TID 1 at $212,000-$213,000 (down from $255,000 due to decreased equalized valuation), TID 2 over $1,034,000 (up from $954,000), and TID 4 at $147,000. He noted debt restructuring freed up $863,000 in principal for TID 2, accelerating its potential closure. Once the distribution center in TID 1 is fully built out, it is projected to generate an additional $444,000 in annual tax increment, potentially paying back the $2.8 million general fund advance well before the 2044 maximum life. The board discussed adding interest charges to the inter-fund advance, with Jacobs noting the LGIP rate (approximately 3.25-3.5%) could be used.

discussions.item: Capital Improvement Program Borrowing and 2028 Debt Service Preview
discussions.body: Jacobs walked the board through a preliminary debt service analysis for a proposed $1,950,000 borrowing (including closing costs) at an estimated 4.75% over 20 years, mirroring a September 2024 Rothschild borrowing. The analysis showed existing debt service could increase from approximately $735,000 levied in 2027 to approximately $873,000 in 2028, representing roughly a 20-cent tax rate increase. Jacobs stressed this does not affect the 2027 budget but will need to be planned for in 2028. He noted the village has no existing debt beyond 2033. Trustee [inaudible] suggested exploring bank financing similar to prior practice rather than bond issuance.

discussions.item: 2028 Budget Pros and Cons
discussions.body: Jacobs verbally presented a list of anticipated 2028 budget factors. Pros included: increased building permit revenue from new subdivisions, potential diesel price decrease eliminating the ~$30/household garbage fuel surcharge, higher highway aid formula funding from infrastructure investment, significantly higher net new construction valuation post-revaluation, no board salary overlap increases, reduced attorney fees as a goal, no three-month court clerk overlap cost, and no revaluation cost ($190,000/year savings). Cons included: projected sewer utility rate increase, deputy clerk moving to 12-month funding, four elections in a presidential year, higher building inspection costs, 20-cent debt service increase, and need to replenish the capital replacement fund.

discussions.item: Contingency Fund Vote
discussions.body: Guy Fidel moved to reduce the contingency fund from the proposed $70,000 to $30,000, arguing residents face hardship and a reduction would build board credibility. The motion failed for lack of a second. APC member Chris Clutes then moved to recommend keeping the contingency at $60,000, seconded by Mary Solheim; the APC recommendation passed. Erin Mishka then moved at the village board level to keep the contingency at $60,000, seconded by Solheim. The motion passed; Jacobs noted the reduction from $70,000 to $60,000 lowers the tax rate from $4.26 to $4.20 and saves approximately $12 on a $200,000 home's village portion.

title: Board Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors held its adjourned organizational meeting on October 20th, covering awards to the Medical Examiner's Office, a new infrastructure committee chair appointment, and an extended debate over a $55 million highway facility project. The board ultimately approved the highway facility resolution as amended, with the amendment requiring a property divestment strategy for the existing West Street site with a goal of returning it to the tax rolls.
